title: Biotechnology
standard_text: Biotechnology uses living things and DNA techniques (cutting and joining DNA, PCR, gel electrophoresis, DNA profiling) in medicine, agriculture and forensics; benefits, risks and ethics. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 10, Quarter 4: Life Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 4: Life Science): mutations, cutting and joining DNA, pCR, gel electrophoresis and DNA profiling and uses and ethics of biotechnology. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: PCR doubles DNA each cycle: 2ⁿ copies after n cycles.
key_sub: In a gel, small fragments move further.
body_html:
How to think about it

Mutations change the DNA sequence. A substitution may change one amino acid (or none: silent); an insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame. Mutations are the source of new alleles.

Gene technology uses restriction enzymes to cut DNA and ligase to join it, for example into a plasmid. PCR copies DNA (2ⁿ copies after n cycles). Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size, as in DNA profiling. CRISPR-Cas9 edits a chosen sequence.

Example

1 DNA molecule, 10 PCR cycles. Copies?

2¹⁰

Answer: 1,024

Example

3,000 bp DNA cut at 1,200. Fragments?

1,200 and 3,000 − 1,200

Answer: 1,200 bp and 1800 bp

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all mutations are harmful.
  • Saying larger DNA fragments move further in a gel.
  • Forgetting that PCR needs primers and a heat-stable polymerase.

faq.q: Why is a frameshift mutation usually worse than a substitution?
faq.a: It changes every codon after the mutation, so many amino acids change and a stop codon may appear early.
Short tandem repeats are copied by PCR and separated by size; the pattern of bands identifies people for forensics and paternity testing.

items.q: What are the three temperature steps in each PCR cycle?
items.e: A heat-stable polymerase (Taq) is used.

items.q: What is a stem cell?
c: an undifferentiated cell that can divide and become specialized
items.e: Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent cells.

items.q:
Mark compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: GGGCGCATATAT
After: GGGGCATATAT
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: A base was removed, so the sequence is shorter.

items.q:
Isabel compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: ATATCGCGA
After: ATACGCGA
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: A base was removed, so the sequence is shorter.

items.q: What do restriction enzymes do?
c: cut DNA at specific base sequences
items.e: They often leave sticky ends.

items.q: mRNA: GUUAUUGUU. Codons: AUU = Ile, GUU = Val. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: GUU AUU GUU.

items.q: What is a point mutation?
c: a change in a single base, by substitution, insertion or deletion
the loss of a whole chromosome
a change in the number of chromosome sets
a change in a protein only
items.e: Sickle-cell anemia is caused by one base substitution.

items.q: mRNA: CAUAGCUGG. Codons: AGC = Ser, CAU = His, UGG = Trp, UUU = Phe, AAU = Asn. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CAU AGC UGG.

items.q: mRNA: AAAAAUGAU. Codons: AAA = Lys, AAU = Asn, GAU = Asp, CGU = Arg, GUU = Val. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AAA AAU GAU.

items.q:
Kenneth compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: TGGATCCTTTA
After: TGGATCCCTTTA
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: An extra base was added, so the sequence is longer.

items.q: What is a silent mutation?
c: a mutation that stops all transcription
a mutation that changes many amino acids
a base change that does not change the amino acid, because the code is degenerate
items.e: The protein is unchanged.

items.q: How does estrogen switch on a gene?
c: it diffuses into the cell and binds to a receptor, releasing a transcription factor
items.e: The factor can then bind to DNA.

items.q: mRNA: UCUAGCUGG. Codons: AGC = Ser, UCU = Ser, UGG = Trp, UUC = Phe, ACU = Thr. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: UCU AGC UGG.

items.q:
Dennis compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: ACCGCATAGGA
After: ACCGCATGGA
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: A base was removed, so the sequence is shorter.

items.q: What does siRNA do?
c: guides an enzyme to cut a complementary mRNA
items.e: The mRNA cannot then be translated.

items.q: Which stem cells can become any type of cell, including placenta?
items.e: Found in the early embryo.

items.q: What is the role of PCR?
c: to make millions of copies of a DNA sequence
items.e: Each cycle doubles the DNA.

items.q: What is an oncogene?
c: a gene that stops cell division
a mutated proto-oncogene that is permanently switched on
items.e: It causes cells to divide too fast.

items.q: Why does an insertion or deletion of one base usually have a big effect?
c: it changes only one amino acid
it shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
items.e: This is a frameshift mutation.

items.q: Why are mutations important for evolution?
c: they are the original source of new alleles and genetic variation
items.e: Most are neutral; some are harmful, a few helpful.

items.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
c: it is not denatured at high temperatures
items.e: It comes from a bacterium in hot springs.

items.q: How is DNA profiling used in forensic science?
c: comparing the lengths of short tandem repeats from crime-scene DNA and suspects
reading a person's whole genome every time
items.e: STR patterns are almost unique to each person.

items.q: What is gene therapy?
c: inserting a working allele into cells to treat a genetic disorder
items.e: Somatic therapy is not passed to children.

items.q: What is genetic fingerprinting based on?
c: genes that are the same in everyone
variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), which differ between people
items.e: The pattern of bands is compared.

items.q: Why are bacteria treated with calcium ions and heat shock in genetic engineering?
c: to make the cell wall and membrane more permeable to plasmids
items.e: This is transformation.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with genetic testing?
c: privacy: insurers or employers might use the results
items.e: Genetic counseling helps people decide.

items.q: Why is PCR heated to about 95 °C?
c: to separate the DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
items.e: Primers anneal at about 55 °C; extension at 72 °C.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1,200 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 400, 600, 650. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighboring positions (including 0 and 1,200): 550, 400, 200, 50. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 300, 450. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighboring positions (including 0 and 1,000): 550, 300, 150. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What does in vivo gene cloning use?
c: vectors such as plasmids to put genes into host cells
items.e: In vitro cloning uses PCR.

items.q: How can genetically modified bacteria make human insulin?
c: the human insulin gene is put into a plasmid and inserted into the bacteria
bacteria are fused with human cells
items.e: The bacteria are grown in fermenters.

items.e: Subtract neighboring positions (including 0 and 2,000): 1,700, 300. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What is personalized medicine?
c: treatment chosen to suit a person's genome
items.e: Genome sequencing makes it possible.

items.q: What are primers in PCR?
c: short single strands of DNA that bind to the start of the target sequence
RNA molecules that carry amino acids
items.e: DNA polymerase starts from them.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 5 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 125 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 25 cycles; amount × 225 = 33,554,432.

items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 2 × 212 = 8,192.

items.q: In gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode?
c: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
they are attracted by the dye
items.e: Smaller fragments move further.

items.q: PCR starts with 2 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 30 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 2 × 230 = 2.15 × 109.

items.q: What does DNA ligase do?
c: joins DNA fragments by forming bonds between nucleotides
items.e: It seals a gene into a plasmid.

items.q: Why is a promoter added with a gene in genetic engineering?
c: so RNA polymerase can bind and the gene is transcribed
items.e: A terminator is added to stop it.

c: a bacterial plasmid with a gene from another organism inserted into it
items.e: Used to make insulin in bacteria.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence CAACCGGTGTAT. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: How does increased methylation of DNA affect a gene?
c: it stops transcription factors binding, so the gene is switched off
items.e: Methyl groups are added to cytosine.

items.q: What does an inversion mutation do?
items.e: The bases are the same but in reverse order.

items.q: Why are marker genes used in genetic engineering?
c: to identify cells that have taken up the recombinant DNA
to make the gene work faster
items.e: For example antibiotic resistance or fluorescence.

items.q: What is the difference between benign and malignant tumors?
c: benign tumors spread around the body
malignant tumors invade tissues and spread (metastasis)
items.e: Benign tumors are usually enclosed.

items.q: What is RNA interference (RNAi)?
c: small RNA molecules bind to mRNA and stop it being translated
items.e: siRNA and miRNA are involved.

items.q: What does DNA ligase do?
c: joins sugar–phosphate backbones of DNA fragments
items.e: It seals sticky ends together.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence ATCTCGTTCATA. What is the probe's sequence?

items.q: How can a substitution mutation stop a protein working?
c: it always makes the protein longer
it may change an amino acid in the active site so the shape changes
items.e: Or it may create a stop codon.

items.q: Why can different cells in one body make different proteins?
c: different genes are switched on (expressed) in each cell type
items.e: All body cells have the same genome.
